book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: The Core Argument
title: The Core Argument
answer: AI adoption in schools fails or succeeds in predictable ways, and the deciding factor is how people lead it. It fails when leaders mandate tools they do not use, reward logins instead of student results, and skip governance, and it succeeds when leaders model AI in their own work, tie incentives to hours saved and student outcomes, and publish clear rules. The core argument is that adoption is a leadership and culture problem, not a purchasing problem.

sections.body: This idea says that whether AI takes hold in a school depends less on which tools are bought than on how leaders behave and what the district rewards. Adoption fails in predictable patterns: leaders mandate tools without using them, districts count logins and licenses rather than results for students, and governance is skipped so tools spread with no rules for privacy, review, and accountability. It succeeds in equally predictable patterns: leaders show staff their own AI use and what they learned, incentives attach to hours saved and student outcomes rather than activity, and districts publish their rules so everyone knows what is allowed, what is required, and who decides. The problem it solves is performative adoption, where a district buys licenses, announces initiatives, and reports impressive usage numbers while nothing changes for students. Staff then comply on paper and ignore the tools in practice, which wastes money and breeds cynicism that makes real change harder.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, this idea plays out through what leaders do visibly and what the district measures. Leaders model use by showing staff how they use AI in their own work and what they have learned, which gives teachers a concrete example rather than a directive. Incentives are tied to hours saved and student outcomes, not to activity, so the reward follows real change instead of logins. Districts publish their rules so everyone knows what is allowed, what is required, and who decides, which turns governance into shared information rather than a hidden process. The text does not give grade band examples, so the practice applies across a school or district as a whole.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as research on school leaders that supports the view. A study of German school leaders found that a digital mindset, marked by agility and empathy, along with leadership that balances exploring new approaches with improving existing ones, predicted how far AI was implemented in their schools (Pietsch & Mah, 2024). A study of Israeli principals spreading a national AI policy found that they relied on professional learning, shared leadership, and ties with parents and partners (Avidov-Ungar & Ganon-Shilon, 2026). The book's summary of both findings is that leaders who engage deeply get further.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out the limits and risks as the predictable failure patterns and the danger of performative adoption. Mandating tools without personal use, rewarding usage counts such as logins and licenses instead of results for students, and skipping governance all undermine adoption, and skipping governance in particular leaves privacy, review, and accountability without rules. Performative adoption is the danger to avoid: a district can buy licenses, announce initiatives, and report impressive usage numbers while nothing changes for students, and staff learn to comply on paper and ignore the tools in practice. The decisions that stay with people are the leadership choices: whether leaders model use, what incentives are tied to, and what rules are published and who decides them. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
